analysis.one_liner: Presumes disabled coal miners who filed black lung claims decades ago qualify for benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in a House subcommittee until the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed the Black Lung Benefits Program for a specific group: coal miners (or their survivors) who filed claims between July 1, 1973 and April 1, 1980 and worked at least 10 years in the mines. Instead of requiring miners to prove they are totally disabled by black lung disease, the bill would have presumed they qualify if any single piece of medical evidence — one positive X-ray, breathing test, blood gas test, or a physician's opinion — showed respiratory impairment. It would also have barred agencies from demanding a higher standard of proof. In practice, that would have shifted thousands of old, often-doubted claims from denial toward approval.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners with 10 or more years in the mines who filed black lung claims in that seven-year window, and the surviving spouses or dependents of miners who died, would have gained monthly disability and survivor benefits without having to fight through repeated medical challenges. The presumption would have applied only to that older group of claims, not to new ones.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Older coal miners and their widows

how_it_helps.text: Miners who filed claims between July 1, 1973 and April 1, 1980 and worked at least 10 years in coal mines would be presumed totally disabled by pneumoconiosis if any qualifying medical evidence existed, ending years of adversarial re-litigation of their condition [S3].

Any single positive test — one X-ray, one set of breathing studies, one set of blood gas studies — or a documented physician's opinion would be enough to invoke the presumption, and the bill explicitly forbids requiring proof by a preponderance of the evidence or any higher standard [S3].
The bill covers death claims too: a miner's death would be presumed due to black lung disease, opening survivor benefits for families whose claims were previously rejected [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Black lung benefits for miners disabled by dust after the 1969 law are paid by coal operators and their insurers rather than general taxpayers, so the companies responsible for miners' exposure would have borne the cost of newly approved claims for this older group.

drawbacks.text: The presumption is strong medicine: a single positive test or one physician's opinion would be enough to win benefits, with the bill explicitly waiving the normal preponderance-of-the-evidence standard, which could let some claims succeed on thin or old evidence [S3].

The bill reaches back over the decade-old deadline of April 1, 1980 to reopen claims from a specific historical window, a retroactive change that would be hard to administer and could re-open determinations already long final [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the miners and families affected, the bill addressed a real historical grievance: claims filed in the 1970s were routinely denied for lack of proof, and the bill would have replaced that burden with a simple presumption. The cost is that the looser evidentiary rule — one test, no higher standard of proof — would approve some claims where the medical link to black lung was genuinely uncertain, and the expense falls on coal operators for a workforce that has long since left the mines. The bill was written narrowly (only the 1973–1980 filing window, only miners with 10+ years of coal work), which limits both its benefit and its cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and passed to a subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markups, and no vote until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Kanjorski introduced the bill on February 11, 1999 [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day; no other member signed on as a cosponsor [S5] [S4].
On March 5, 1999 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and the record shows no further action of any kind [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2001 with the bill still stalled in subcommittee, so it died without a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal operators and their insurers are better off, because the liability for thousands of older black lung claims expired with the bill. The miners and widows who filed claims between 1973 and 1980 got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal operators; miners and widows got nothing

for.name: Rep. Paul Kanjorski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; no other member cosponsored it.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections on March 5, 1999 and never held a hearing or reported it back to the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a vote, so no record shows how the parties would have split; a Pennsylvania Democrat introduced it and no one else signed on.

industries.industry: Coal mining operators and their insurers
industries.note: Under the black lung program, benefits for miners exposed after the 1969 law are paid by the responsible coal company, so the bill would have converted hundreds or thousands of old denied claims into a paying liability. Their interest in keeping old claims denied runs directly against the disabled miners the bill served.

industries.industry: Coal miners and their surviving families
industries.note: Miners with 10 or more years underground who filed claims in the 1973–1980 window would have won a presumption of total disability from black lung, and their widows and dependents would have gained survivor benefits.
